paragraphs.text: MAGIS syndrome is a multisystem developmental disorder with immune dysregulation. It is caused by heterozygous germline activating mutations in GNAI2, which encodes the heterotrimeric G-protein subunit G-alpha-i2. Its 5 cardinal features are midline malformations of the brain, anterior pituitary gland dysfunction, growth retardation, immunodysregulation/immunodeficiency, and skeletal defects. Expression is highly variable, even among relatives carrying the same mutation. Immune involvement includes susceptibility to a broad range of infections, autoimmunity, and autoinflammation (Ham et al., 2024; Lamborn et al., 2025).

paragraphs.text: Ham et al. (2024) studied 20 patients from 18 unrelated families of diverse ancestries (Latino/Admixed American, non-Finnish European, Finnish European, West Sub-Saharan African, and Middle Eastern Arab). Developmental abnormalities included intrauterine growth retardation, dysmorphism, bone dysostosis, neuroanatomic abnormalities, and birth defects in other organs. Dysmorphic features included frontal prominence, flat face, high anterior hairline, and sandal gap. Midline structural defects were observed, most commonly congenital nasal septum deviation, dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, pituitary hypoplasia with growth hormone deficiency, Chiari I malformation, micropenis, sagittal cleft ('butterfly') vertebrae, and scoliosis. Some patients had rare birth defects, including subcortical band heterotopia, agenesis of the olfactory bulbs, and coloboma. Other findings included brachydactyly type E, swan-neck deformity, misshapen sella turcica, diffuse leukodystrophy progressing to end-stage neurodegeneration, hippocampal malrotation, cerebellar dysplasia, polymicrogyria, subependymal heterotopia, and intestinal malrotation. Most patients also had postnatal abnormalities, including short stature with neurodevelopmental delay, neurobehavioral deficits, and gastrointestinal dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Nearly all (90%) of the patients reported by Ham et al. (2024) had immune involvement, with recurrent, unusual, and/or severe infections. Skin infections were prominent and included bacterial, superficial fungal, or unusually severe viral infections such as recurrent shingles, extensive warts, and rubella vaccine-associated skin granulomas. Respiratory, middle ear, and sinus infections were common, some patients developed bronchiectasis, and some had invasive bacterial infections. Inflammatory or autoimmune complications included lymphocytic infiltration of organs, psoriasis, discoid lupus, autoimmune cytopenias with splenomegaly, Hashimoto thyroiditis, type I diabetes mellitus, colitis, and macrophage activation syndrome. Several patients had asthma or atopic dermatitis. Laboratory studies showed monocytosis and neutrophilia that were precipitated by acute infection and persisted in some patients. T-cell counts were initially low, with decreased recent thymic emigrants and a paucity of naive versus effector/memory T cells, but rose with age. Lymphocyte proliferation and activation were normal or even increased. Dysgammaglobulinemia, with low serum IgM and poorer vaccine titers, was accompanied by decreased B-cell counts and atretic lymphoid follicles in secondary lymphoid organs. Patients with mutations at thr182 had greater immune involvement because of additional inflammatory or autoimmune complications.

paragraphs.text: Lamborn et al. (2025) reviewed the features of the 20 patients reported by Ham et al. (2024). Growth retardation was the most penetrant feature (90%) and included prenatal intrauterine growth restriction (53%) and postnatal short stature (90%). Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 was low in 8 of 11 patients tested, and growth hormone deficiency was found in all 7 patients formally tested. Structural (41%) or functional (53%) defects of the anterior pituitary gland were present in 59% of patients. Excluding pituitary and sella turcica defects, 30% had midline brain malformations, including agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, cerebellar hypoplasia, pons hypoplasia, and Chiari I malformation. Skeletal defects, comprising craniofacial, appendicular, and axial dysostoses, affected 85% of patients, and dysmorphism was present in all (100%). Patients could also have cardiovascular, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and dermatologic disease. Lamborn et al. (2025) stated that extremely rare features, such as coloboma or subcortical band heterotopia, should raise suspicion of MAGIS.

paragraphs.text: Lamborn et al. (2025) also summarized the immune features. Immune-mediated disease was present in 95% of patients, including immunodeficiency (90%) and immune dysregulation (50%). Immune dysregulation comprised systemic autoinflammation (15%), autoimmunity (35%), and splenomegaly (35%). Infections involved the respiratory tract (75%), middle ear (65%), sinuses (35%), and skin (25%), and invasive infections included meningitis (10%), bacteremia (20%), and cutaneous abscess (15%). Twenty-five percent of patients were extensively affected by cutaneous viral infections, mainly human papillomavirus-related warts. Some individual patients had life-threatening lymphocytic infiltration of the brain, lung, or liver, or macrophage activation syndrome. Autoimmune manifestations included autoimmune hemolytic anemia (20%), autoimmune thrombocytopenia (10%), and psoriasis (10%), as well as Hashimoto thyroiditis, type I diabetes mellitus, alopecia, celiac disease, and autoimmune enteritis in individual patients. Hypogammaglobulinemia affected 20% of patients. Myelokathexis was not observed, although only 3 patients had bone marrow examination, and neutropenia was seen only intermittently in 1 critically ill patient. Newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency was abnormal in 1 patient (P13), whose absolute T-cell count was 0.577 x 10(3) cells/microliter at 7 weeks of age and 1.486 x 10(3) cells/microliter 1 month later. Premature mortality in the original cohort of 20 patients was 10%.

paragraphs.text: In 20 patients from 18 unrelated families with MAGIS, Ham et al. (2024) identified heterozygous missense mutations in the GNAI2 gene by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. The index patient was studied by trio exome sequencing with an unaffected sib. Other patients were found through GeneMatcher or through inquiries driven by immune phenotype, and the familial mutation in 1 patient was identified by Sanger sequencing. The variants were predicted to be deleterious (CADD score greater than 25). They were absent from the Greater Middle Eastern Variome and gnomAD v3.1.2, except for R179H, which was found in 1 individual of unknown affection status. Twelve mutations had occurred de novo. Patient cells expressed equal amounts of mutant and wildtype transcripts and normal levels of total G-alpha-i2 protein. The mutated residues were evolutionarily conserved and clustered in the Ras-like GTPase domain, particularly the P-loop and switch regions. Most mutant proteins bound GTP-gamma-S more readily than wildtype, R179H being the exception. All showed decreased GTP hydrolysis, and all except R179H were resistant to the GTPase-activating effect of RGS16. Overexpressed mutant proteins suppressed forskolin-induced cAMP production, and patient fibroblasts produced less cAMP. Ham et al. (2024) concluded that these were activating mutations. No other candidate gene was shared among the patients.

paragraphs.text: Ham et al. (2024) found that CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from several patients showed decreased chemotaxis toward multiple chemokines, and T cells from 1 patient tested had reduced chemokine-induced calcium fluxes. Expressing the mutant proteins in healthy donor T cells reproduced these defects, except for I55M, and L38R and R179C had intermediate, more variable effects. Patient neutrophils also showed reduced directional migration. In 1 patient, leukocytes accumulated poorly in the oral mucosa and in induced skin blisters. In mice, T cells expressing mutant G-alpha-i2 migrated less well into lymph nodes and splenic white pulp after adoptive transfer. Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer studies showed that activated mutant G-alpha-i2 interacted minimally with chemokine receptors at steady state. Knockout of adenylyl cyclases AC3 or AC7 in T cells did not affect chemotaxis, indicating that the migration defect was independent of cAMP.

paragraphs.text: Ham et al. (2024) found that patient T cells showed increased activation and proliferation after T-cell receptor (TCR) stimulation. Proximal TCR signaling was normal, but RAS activation and downstream ERK/MAPK and PI3K-AKT-S6 signaling were enhanced. CRISPR-Cas9 deletion of the mutant GNAI2 allele in T cells from 1 patient restored normal responses, and expressing T182A or Q205L G-alpha-i2 in healthy donor T cells reproduced the hyperresponsiveness. By proteomic analysis, Ham et al. (2024) identified RASA2, a RAS GTPase-activating protein, as an interactor that bound activated G-alpha-i2 more strongly than wildtype. Activated G-alpha-i2 did not directly inhibit RASA2 GAP activity. Instead, it redistributed RASA2 toward the plasma membrane, and RAS activation at the Golgi was enhanced. The T-cell hyperactivation was independent of cAMP. Ham et al. (2024) proposed that the resulting increase in TCR signaling breaks peripheral tolerance and predisposes patients to autoimmunity. Because of the activated RAS-MAPK signaling, they suggested that the disorder falls within the RASopathy spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Lamborn et al. (2025) recommended a full immunologic workup for patients with MAGIS, including quantitative immunoglobulins and vaccine titers. They advised considering immunoglobulin replacement in patients with low total IgG, nonprotective vaccine responses, or persistent infections. One patient received hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) from a fully matched unrelated donor and achieved full donor chimerism. HSCT eradicated his granulomatous skin disease caused by vaccine-strain rubella virus, as well as his recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, otitis media, and bronchitis. His autoimmune hemolytic anemia remained in remission for more than 3 years, although he received immunosuppressants for chronic graft-versus-host disease. HSCT did not affect his nonimmune features, including autism spectrum disorder and growth hormone deficiency. In vitro, inhibitors of the RAS/ERK/MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways each partially corrected T-cell hyperresponsiveness, and the 2 together corrected it completely. Lamborn et al. (2025) suggested gene therapy, inhibitors of these downstream pathways such as sirolimus, or phosphodiesterase inhibitors as possible treatments. They considered WHIM-specific drugs such as plerixafor or mavorixafor unlikely to be useful.
